research_question: What is the effect of metformin added to megestrol acetate, compared with megestrol acetate alone, on complete regression of endometrial hyperplasia (with or without atypia) in women with endometrial hyperplasia?
outcome_description: Complete regression of endometrial hyperplasia to normal endometrium (proliferative, secretory, or atrophic) at the end of treatment
positive_direction: An odds ratio greater than 1 favors metformin plus megestrol acetate (indicating higher rates of endometrial hyperplasia regression)
search_queries: metformin megestrol acetate endometrial hyperplasia trial
metformin megestrol regression endometrial hyperplasia comparison
metformin megestrol controlled trial endometrial hyperplasia
inclusion_criteria: Studies evaluating adult women diagnosed with endometrial hyperplasia (with or without atypia).
Studies directly comparing the combination of metformin and megestrol acetate versus megestrol acetate alone.
Studies reporting quantitative data on complete regression to normal endometrium (proliferative, secretory, or atrophic) at the end of treatment.
exclusion_criteria: Not an original empirical study (systematic reviews, meta-analyses, narrative reviews, editorials, commentaries, or theoretical papers).

No direct comparison between metformin combined with megestrol acetate and megestrol acetate alone (e.g., studies evaluating metformin monotherapy, levonorgestrel intrauterine systems, or single-arm designs).
No quantitative outcome data allowing calculation of an effect size for endometrial hyperplasia regression (such as event counts, proportions, or odds ratios).
Completely unrelated to endometrial hyperplasia or the interventions of interest.
moderators_to_extract: Hyperplasia atypia status (atypical endometrial hyperplasia vs non-atypical)
Treatment duration (e.g., 3 months vs 6 months vs longer)
Study design (randomized controlled trial vs non-randomized comparative study)
effect_size_note: Outcome pooled as odds ratio (OR) based on dichotomous events of regression to normal endometrium versus persistent/progressed disease.
